{{Short description|Early form of the Burmese language}} {{Infobox language | name = Old Burmese | region = [[Pagan Kingdom]] | era = 12th–16th centuries | image = Myazedi-Inscription-Burmese-cropped.png | imagecaption = Detail of the Myazedi inscription | familycolor = Sino-Tibetan | fam2 = ([[Tibeto-Burman languages|Tibeto-Burman]]) | fam3 = [[Lolo–Burmese languages|Lolo–Burmese]] | fam4 = [[Burmish languages|Burmish]] | script = [[Burmese script]] | iso3 = obr | linglist = obr | glotto = oldb1235 | glottorefname = Old Burmese }} {{Contains special characters|Burmese}} '''Old Burmese''' was an early form of the [[Burmese language]], as attested in the stone inscriptions of [[Bagan|Pagan]], and is the oldest phase of Burmese linguistic history. The transition to [[Middle Burmese]] occurred in the 16th century.{{cite book|last=Herbert|first=Patricia|author2=Anthony Crothers Milner|title=South-East Asia: Languages and Literatures: a Select Guide|publisher=University of Hawaii Press|year=1989|pages=5|isbn=9780824812676}} The transition to Middle Burmese included phonological changes (e.g. mergers of [[Minimal pair|sound pairs]] that were distinct in Old Burmese) as well as accompanying changes in the underlying [[orthography]]. [[Word order]], grammatical structure and vocabulary have remained markedly comparable, well into Modern Burmese, with the exception of lexical content (e.g. [[function word]]s).{{cite book|last=Wheatley|first=Julian|editor1=Randy J. LaPolla |editor2=Graham Thurgood|title=Sino-Tibetan Languages|chapter=12. Burmese|publisher=Routledge|year=2013|isbn=9781135797171}} ==Phonology== Unlike most [[Tibeto-Burman languages]], Burmese has a phonological system with two-way aspiration: [[preaspiration]] (e.g. {{lang|my|မှ}} ''hma.'' vs. {{lang|my|မ}} ''ma.'') and [[Aspirated consonant|postaspiration]] (e.g. {{lang|my|ခ}} ''kha.'' vs. {{lang|my|က}} ''ka.'').{{cite book|last=Yanson|first=Rudolf A.|title=Aspiration in the Burmese Phonological System: A Diachronic Account|editor=Nathan W. Hill|publisher=Brill|year=2012|series=Medieval Tibeto-Burman Languages IV|pages=17–29|isbn=9789004232020}} In Burmese, this distinction serves to differentiate [[causative|causative and non-causative]] verbs of Sino-Tibetan etymology. In Old Burmese, postaspiration can be reconstructed to the proto-Burmese language, whereas preaspiration is comparatively newer, having derived from proto-prefixes. The merging of proto-prefixes (i.e., {{lang|my|ဟ}} as an independent consonant used as a prefix) to preaspirated consonants was nearly complete by the 12th century. ==Orthography== Old Burmese maintains a number of distinctions which are no longer present in the orthography of standard Burmese. ===Diacritics=== Whereas Modern Standard Burmese uses 3 written medials ({{IPA|/-y-/}}, {{IPA|/-w-/}}, and {{IPA|/-r-/}}), Old Burmese had a fourth written medial {{IPA|/-l-/}}, which was typically written as a stacked consonant {{lang|my|္လ}} underneath the letter being modified. Old Burmese orthography treated the preaspirated consonant as a separate segment, since a special [[diacritic]] (''ha hto'', {{lang|my|ှ}}) had not yet been innovated. As such, the letter ''ha'' ({{lang|my|ဟ}}) was stacked above the consonant being modified (e.g. {{lang|my|ဟ္မ}} where Modern Burmese uses {{lang|my|မှ}}). ===Gloss=== Examples of such differences include the consonant ''yh-'' and the lateral clusters ''kl-'' and ''khl-''. The earliest Old Burmese documents, in particular the Myazedi and [[Lokatheikpan]] inscriptions frequently have ''-o-'' where later Burmese has ''-wa''. {{cite journal | last = Hill | first = Nathan W. | title = Three notes on Laufer's law | journal = Linguistics of the Tibeto-Burman Area | volume = 36 | issue = 1 | pages = 57–72 | date = 2013 | url = http://eprints.soas.ac.uk/15932 }} Old Burmese also had a final ''-at'' and ''-an'' distinct from ''-ac'' and ''-any'' as shown by Nishi (1974). {| class="wikitable" |- ! Examples include: *"widow" - Mon {{lang|mnw|{{Script/mnw-Mymr|ကၟဲာ}}}} > Burmese {{lang|my|kamay}} *"excrement" - Mon {{lang|mnw|{{Script/mnw-Mymr|...}}}} > Burmese {{lang|my|haruk}} *"sun" - Mon {{lang|mnw|{{Script/mnw-Mymr|တ္ၚဲ}}}} > Burmese {{lang|my|taŋuy}} Moreover, Mon influenced Old Burmese orthography, particularly with regard to preference for certain spelling conventions: *use of -E- ({{lang|my|-ဧ-}}) instead of -Y- ({{lang|my|ျ}}) (e.g. "destroy" {{lang|my|ဖဧက်}}, not {{lang|my|ဖျက်}} as in modern Burmese) *use of RH- ({{lang|my|ဟြ > ရှ}}) instead of HR- as done with other preaspirated consonants (e.g. "monk" {{lang|my|ရှင်}}, not {{lang|my|ဟြင်}}) - attributed to the fact that Old Mon did not have preaspirated consonants ==Grammar== Two grammatical markers presently found in Modern Burmese are extant to Old Burmese: *{{lang|my|၏}} - finite predicate (placed at the end of a sentence) *{{lang|my|၍}} - nonfinite predicate (conjunction that connects two clauses) In Old Burmese, {{lang|my|၍}} was spelt ''ruy-e''({{lang|my|ရုယ်}}), following the pattern in [[Pali]], whose inflected verbs can express the main predicate. Pali also had an influence in the construction of written Old Burmese [[Grammatical modifier|verbal modifiers]]. Whereas in Modern Burmese, the verb + {{lang|my|သော}} (''sau:'') construction can only modify the succeeding noun (e.g. {{lang|my|ချစ်သောလူ}}, "man who loves") and {{lang|my|သူ}} (''su'') can only modify the preceding verb (e.g. {{lang|my|ချစ်သူ}}, "lover"), in Old Burmese, both constructions, verb + {{lang|my|သော}} and verb + {{lang|my|သူ}} were interchangeable. This was a consequence of Pali grammar, which dictates that participles can be used in noun functions. Pali grammar also influenced negation in written Old Burmese, as many Old Burmese inscriptions adopt the Pali method of negation. In Burmese, negation is accomplished by prefixing a negative particle {{lang|my|မ}} (''ma.'') to the verb being negated. In Pali, {{lang|my|အ}} (''a.'') is used instead. Such grammatical influences from Pali on written Old Burmese had disappeared by the 15th century. ==Pronouns== {|class="wikitable" |+Pronouns in Old Burmese{{cite journal|last=Bradley|first=David|date=Spring 1993|title=Pronouns in Burmese-Lolo|journal=Linguistics of the Tibeto-Burman Area|publisher=La Trobe University|location=Melbourne|volume=16|issue=1|url=http://sealang.net/sala/archives/pdf4/bradley1993pronouns.pdf}} |- !
